definition: The whole group of people or objects that a statistical question is about.
The part of a population that data is actually collected from, used to draw conclusions about the whole population.
A sample chosen so that every member of the population has the same chance of being picked.
Data that can take only separate values, usually counts, such as the number of goals in a match.
Data that is measured and can take any value in a range, such as a time, a mass or a length.
A built-in tendency of a sampling method to pick some kinds of member more often than others, so the sample misrepresents the population.
A data value more than $1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$ below the lower quartile or above the upper quartile.
The upper quartile minus the lower quartile, $\mathrm{IQR} = Q_{3} - Q_{1}$: the spread of the middle half of the data.
Choosing a sample so that every possible group of the required size is equally likely to be picked, for example by drawing numbers at random from a full list.
Choosing every $k$th member from an ordered list of the population, starting from a randomly chosen member among the first $k$.
Splitting the population into groups by a shared feature, then taking a random sample from each group in proportion to its size.
Setting how many members to take from each group, then letting the collector choose anyone who fits until each number is reached; the choice is not random.
Taking the members of the population that are easiest to reach, such as the first people to arrive.
